items.abstract: Shanidar Cave, Iraqi Kurdistan, is among the most significant Neanderthal sites. Excavations by Ralph Solecki in the 1950s unearthed the remains of at least ten Neanderthals and associated Middle Palaeolithic Mousterian stone tools which have played a crucial role in our understanding of Neanderthal behaviour. Solecki also identified Upper Palaeolithic deposits containing Baradostian tools (broadly equivalent to the Aurignacian industry) separated from the Neanderthal layer by 1 metre of sediment, which he interpreted as reflecting a 10,000-year hiatus. Recent excavations (2015 – present) using single-context excavation, with three-dimensional plotting of all artefacts bigger than 2 cm, have improved our understanding of the site’s inhabitants. Lithics recovered from Shanidar Cave were identified and attributed to typological class. The results of typological analysis show that there is a contextual overlap between typologically Mousterian and Baradostian artefacts, and that there is no evidence for a hiatus in occupation at the site. Blades and bladelets, tool forms not usually associated with Neanderthals, were recovered from secure contexts dating to MIS 5a including from contexts containing Neanderthal skeletal remains. Use-wear analysis conducted using a DINO-LITE Edge digital microscope showed that 106 lithics retain evidence of use. The materials worked include wood, hide, meat and bone, bone, horn and plants. There is no significant difference in worked materials between MIS 5 and MIS 3 at Shanidar Cave. The results of typological analysis at Shanidar Cave suggest that assigning a particular tool industry to a particular hominin group may be problematic, which has implications for the wider region. The results of use-wear analysis suggest that there are no behavioural differences between MIS 5 hominins and MIS 3 hominins at Shanidar.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    In our species’ evolutionary history, the type of environments in which we evolved can provide crucial details about early human adaptive capacities. Such environments might not exist under current climatic and ecological conditions. Reconstructing palaeohydrology and vegetation using multiple proxies at human fossil sites in South Africa provides insights into local conditions at a high level of detail. This paper presents a plant
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    -alkane stable isotope record for Florisbad and Lombard’s Drift, which is anchored by new luminescence ages that revise the age for the Florisbad human cranium. We observe contrasting, non-analog plant environments during the Middle and Late Pleistocene by combining multiple lines of evidence to better understand the different environments that early
                    <jats:italic>Homo sapiens</jats:italic>
                    experienced. It also provides the foundation to evaluate their cultural adaptation strategies through time.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Despite the increasing number of studies undertaking isotopic analyses on archaeological material, some regions of the world and certain research foci remain underresearched and underrepresented. One of these regions is Southeast Asia, where bioarchaeological research was only comparatively recently established compared with other regions of the world. To these ends, this review explores publication and research trends in Southeast Asian bioarchaeology regarding stable isotope analyses of human remains, through a combined bibliometric and content analysis approach of identified in‐scope sources (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 37). Key results of this analysis and review indicate that the rates of matching country affiliation authorship and open access are increasing over time, although some regions still remain underrepresented. Additionally, while many studies discussed issues of diagenesis and sample integrity, only 37.8% of studies directly assessed their samples for diagenetic change. In terms of opportunities, there is scope for further serial sampling or paired tissue studies in the region, along with potential big data approaches, and broader discussions about ethics and equity. These results are tempered by several methodological limitations, including limitation to only sources published in the English language. Moving forward, stable isotope research in Southeast Asia should prioritize quality control measures and diagenesis assessments and work with local researchers and descendant communities. Broadly, this review provides a launch point for future isotopic research in the region.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sauropod dinosaurs achieved unprecedented terrestrial gigantism, raising questions about the biomechanical limits of bone under extreme gravitational loads. We estimated static gravitational pressures (Pg) on appendicular cortical bone in neosauropods, including diplodocoids, brachiosaurids, and titanosaurs. We did this by measuring cortical thickness, estimating body masses, and calculating pressures on limb bones. We compared the results with the theoretical fracture thresholds of composite cortical bone (~150–200 MPa) and pure crystalline hydroxyapatite (~1000 MPa). In the largest specimens, Pg remained two orders of magnitude below the compressive strength of hydroxyapatite. These estimates are a conservative lower bound because they assume simultaneous four‐limb support. They are also substantially lower (>15 MPa) than the functional failure threshold of composite cortical bone. Dynamic behaviors raise these values: during slow locomotion, a single hindlimb may briefly support the entire hindquarter load, and the weight distribution between fore‐ and hindlimbs varies markedly with center‐of‐mass position. Even so, rearing on the hindlimbs in the largest titanosaurs (>25 metric tons) would remain within safe limits defined by composite‐bone failure thresholds. Neosauropod lineages show distinct biomechanical strategies. Diplodocoids kept a posteriorly positioned center of mass compatible with facultative bipedal rearing. Brachiosaurids shifted it cranially through neck and forelimb hypertrophy. Titanosaurs reached extreme sizes through enhanced secondary bone remodeling and extensive postcranial pneumatization. Cortical thickening is consistently associated with increasing gravitational loads across Neosauropoda. However, this static model does not test whether it was the primary evolutionary response, compared with other strategies such as trabecular densification and postcranial pneumaticity.</jats:p>

items.title: Cortical bone geometry and static gravitational loads in neosauropod dinosaurs: Implications for biomechanical constraints on terrestrial gigantism

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The modern human mandibular symphysis displays a mental prominence, a unique trait in the human lineage. Beyond this shared pattern, considerable variability in shape and metrics exists. This heterogeneity is thought to result from multiple mechanisms, including biomechanical compensation, allometric and dietary effects, population genetics, or sexual dimorphism. While the influence of these processes on overall mandibular shape is thoroughly documented, limited information exists on their effects on the distribution of mandibular cortical bone. Thus, this study assessed the impact of local and global allometry, sexual dimorphism, and cortical area on the shape and size of the symphyseal cortical bone contours.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed computed tomography images of 62 modern human mandibles using Elliptic Fourier Descriptors. The effects of the investigated variables on external and internal cortical bone shapes and sizes were tested using a nested multivariate approach and predicted shape reconstructions were used to visualize morphological variation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this sample, sex, and local allometry had significant effects on mandibular symphyseal shape and sex was the main predictor of local allometry. Cortical area significantly affected the shape and size of the external cortical bone contour and body weight influenced the size of the internal cortical bone contour.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sexual dimorphism, allometric effects, and biomechanical compensation impact the shape and size of the mandibular symphysis. External and internal cortical bone contours respond differently to these effects. Future studies could investigate the influence of other relevant factors on symphyseal shape and size.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
